extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the foundation of human life, seeking wisdom on what sustains a person.
Bhishma declares wisdom as the foundation of all beings, the highest attainment, supreme blessing, and heaven for the virtuous.
Bhishma cites examples of Bali, Prahlada, Namuchi, and Mungi who achieved their goals through wisdom after losing wealth.
Bhishma begins recounting an ancient dialogue between Indra and Kashyapa.
Sage Kashyapa, practicing severe austerities, is knocked down by a proud and wealthy Vaishya driving a chariot.
Injured and angry, Kashyapa decides to end his life, declaring that poverty makes life meaningless.
Indra, taking the form of a jackal, approaches the despairing Kashyapa and begins to counsel him.
Indra (as jackal) reminds Kashyapa that all creatures desire human birth, and among humans, Brahmin status is most coveted.

attributes.argument: Kashyapa possesses what others desire most

extraction_text: Indra criticizes Kashyapa's ingratitude, noting he has achieved the difficult status of a Veda-knowing Brahmin yet wants to die without cause.
Indra explains that all attainments breed pride, and Kashyapa's discontent stems from greed despite apparent satisfaction.

attributes.observation: Pride and greed as sources of discontent

extraction_text: Indra contrasts human hands (which they lack as jackals) with Kashyapa's desire for wealth, emphasizing the greater importance of physical capabilities.

attributes.contrast: Hands vs. wealth, physical capability vs. material possession

extraction_text: Indra describes the suffering of animals without hands or tongues who cannot remove thorns, drive away insects, or protect themselves from elements.

attributes.perspective: Animal suffering compared to human privilege

extraction_text: Indra lists the miseries of various animal births (jackals, insects, rats, snakes, frogs) that Kashyapa has fortunately avoided.

attributes.argument: Kashyapa should be grateful for his human Brahmin birth

extraction_text: Indra states that despite being eaten by insects without hands to drive them away, he doesn't abandon life to avoid worse rebirths.

attributes.lesson: Endurance despite suffering to avoid worse fate

extraction_text: Indra observes that some creatures experience more pleasure, others more pain, but no creature experiences complete happiness.

attributes.truth: Universal nature of mixed happiness and suffering

extraction_text: Indra describes the endless cycle of human desire: from wealth to kingdom, to divinity, to lordship of gods, with satisfaction always elusive.
Indra concludes that even if Kashyapa attained wealth, he couldn't become king or god, and even divine status wouldn't bring satisfaction.

attributes.conclusion: No attainment brings ultimate satisfaction; wisdom and gratitude are key

extraction_text: A philosophical discourse on desire, satisfaction, and human nature is presented.
The Speaker argues that acquiring desirable things does not bring satisfaction, and enjoyment only fuels further desire.
The Speaker advises Kashyapa to cut the root of all desires and actions, and to restrain the senses.
The Speaker states that desire arises from contact, sight, and hearing, and that the best way for a person to control themselves is by not tasting, touching, or seeing.
The Speaker describes the paradox of human existence: having hands, wealth, and strength, yet also causing the enslavement of man by man, and enduring suffering while still finding joy.
The Speaker notes that some people, despite having strength, knowledge, and intellect, are forced by their karma into despised and evil professions.
The Speaker points out that even the Pulkasa and Chandala castes, though dissatisfied with their birth, do not abandon themselves, and urges Kashyapa to see this illusion.
The Speaker tells Kashyapa he should be satisfied with his own birth, especially when seeing those who are diseased, maimed, or paralyzed.
The Speaker urges Kashyapa, a Brahmin, to rise up and follow dharma, as he has no real excuse or fault, and promises him the merit of Vedic teachings if he listens.
The Speaker gives specific instructions: be diligent, study the Vedas, maintain sacred fires, be truthful, practice self-control, give alms, and avoid competition.

The Speaker contrasts those who study the Vedas and perform sacrifices (who are happy) with those born at inauspicious times who do not perform sacrifices or produce offspring (who fall into evil wombs).

The Speaker reveals his past: he was a logician who reviled the Vedas, had no faith, doubted everything, was ignorant yet proud, and as a result, received the karmic fruit of being reborn as a jackal.

characters: The Speaker (Unnamed, a Jackal in current life)
attributes.action: Revelation of Past Life and Karmic Consequence

extraction_text: The Speaker (the jackal) states that if, after hundreds of days and nights, he is reborn as a human again, he will be content, diligent, devoted to sacrifices, charity, and austerities, knowing what should be known and abandoning what should be abandoned.
The sage Kashyapa rises and declares to the speaker, 'Indeed, you are wise and intelligent, and you astonish me.'

attributes.relationship_change: Kashyapa is impressed and acknowledges the speaker's wisdom.

extraction_text: The Brahmin carefully examined with his wisdom-eye and recognized him as the husband of Shachi, the king of gods Indra.

attributes.relationships: Indra is identified as the husband of Shachi

extraction_text: Kashyapa worshipped Indra who rides a tawny horse, obtained his permission, and returned to his own hermitage.
This concludes the 173rd chapter of the Shanti Parva in the auspicious Mahabharata.
